meta.location: The land of Moron, Ablom by the seashore, and the land southward
meta.date: From Omer through Heth, and the dearth
meta.unit: Omer's escape, Emer's peace, and the dearth (Ether 9)
principles: A dream that empties one house before the killing
A record that leaves two animal names untranslated
Repentance accepted at the last possible hour

world_behind.title: A dream moves one household
world_behind.text: Verse 3 has the Lord warn Omer in a dream to depart, and he goes. 1 Nephi 2:2 and Omni 1:12 have the two other founding migrations of the record begin the same way, with a warning to a single man to take his household and leave.

world_behind.title: The route is charted by later landmarks
world_behind.text: Verse 3 fixes Omer's path past the hill Shim and the place where the Nephites were destroyed. Mormon 1:3 puts Ammaron's records in the hill Shim and Mormon 6:6 puts Cumorah at the second site, so Moroni is charting a Jaredite escape route by landmarks from his own lifetime.

world_behind.title: Thirty souls come through the civil war
world_behind.text: Verse 12 gives thirty survivors of the civil war, besides those who had fled with the house of Omer. Ether 15:23 to 25 counts the last war down through fifty-two and twenty-seven; a Jaredite kingdom is twice reduced to a number a reader can hold in mind.

world_behind.title: Two animals go unnamed in English
world_behind.text: Verse 19 lists cureloms and cumoms beside elephants.

world_behind.title: Coriantum's dates are given
world_behind.text: Verse 24 has Coriantum's wife die at a hundred and two and puts his own death at a hundred and forty-two. These are the only ages given for anyone in the book of Ether, and the volume records no other lifespan past a hundred.

world_behind.title: Prophets were thrown into pits
world_behind.text: Verse 29 says it was done at the commandment of king Heth.

words.text: A formal hearing granted by a ruler. The record uses the word once, here, and the King James Bible twelve times. Verse 5 has the murder happen during one.
Watchful of a rival, or unwilling to share. It appears three times in the record, and the King James Bible nineteen. Verse 7 applies it to a father toward his son.
An animal name carried over untranslated. The word appears twice in the record, both in this verse, and never in the King James Bible. Cumoms sits beside it on the same terms.
Brought to full growth, and so ready to be taken. Treated at Jacob 5:37. It appears four times in the record and not once in the King James Bible.
An unmarried young woman. The record uses the word four times and the King James Bible thirty-seven.
To remove a king from his seat. Treated at Mosiah 29:21. Four uses here, and none in the King James Bible.
A failure of food, usually from drought. The word turns up twice here, and the King James Bible eight times. Verse 30 pairs it with no rain.

phrases.term: The Lord warned Omer in a dream that he should depart out of the land
phrases.text: The whole rescue, in one clause. No battle is fought for the throne he loses.

phrases.term: Save it were Jared and his family
phrases.text: The exception in the household roll. The son who stayed is the one who takes the crown.

phrases.term: Anointed king over the people, by the hand of wickedness
phrases.text: Moroni marking the anointing as illegitimate while reporting it. The phrase names the hand that did it.

phrases.term: As he sat upon his throne, giving audience to his people
phrases.text: Where the killing happened. The verse places it in the middle of official business.

phrases.term: It had corrupted the hearts of all the people
phrases.text: Moroni's account of how far the society had spread. Verse 12 will count the survivors at thirty.

phrases.term: Kept him upon little or no food until he had suffered death
phrases.text: A son starved in his father's prison, reported in half a verse.

phrases.term: The people of Akish were desirous for gain, even as Akish was desirous for power
phrases.text: Two motives held side by side. Verse 11 has the sons buy what the oath had held.

phrases.term: The Lord began again to take the curse from off the land
phrases.text: The turn between the killing and the prosperity. Verse 16 credits the lifting to the Lord.

phrases.term: There were elephants and cureloms and cumoms
phrases.text: Three names in a list, two of them left in the original. Moroni adds that the last two were especially useful.

phrases.term: He even saw the Son of Righteousness, and did rejoice and glory in his day
phrases.text: What Emer saw before he died. Malachi 4:2 uses the same title of the one who rises with healing.

phrases.term: Some of them they cast into pits and left them to perish
phrases.text: How the prophets of verse 28 were answered. Verse 29 assigns the order to the king.

verses.label: v. 5–7
verses.title: Two killings inside one household, reported flatly
verses.text: The record follows the violence through a family without comment. Akish "sought the life of his father-in-law" and obtained it by the oath of his secret society. Then he turns on his own child: "Akish began to be jealous of his son, therefore he shut him up in prison, and kept him upon little or no food until he had suffered death." The method is starvation and the motive is jealousy, and both are stated in one sentence. No judgment is passed on either killing in the verse that reports it.

verses.label: v. 11–12
verses.title: A civil war explained as a bidding contest
verses.text: The record gives the two sides different motives and makes the mismatch the cause: "the people of Akish were desirous for gain, even as Akish was desirous for power; wherefore, the sons of Akish did offer them money, by which means they drew away the more part of the people after them." Power on one side, money on the other, and the side with money wins the following. Verse 12 states the cost with a number: the war ran "unto the destruction of nearly all the people of the kingdom, yea, even all, save it were thirty souls."

verses.label: v. 24–25
verses.title: Two ages given, and one of them is unusual
verses.text: The record supplies figures for domestic events that no summary would keep: "his wife died, being an hundred and two years old," and then Coriantum "took to wife, in his old age, a young maid, and begat sons and daughters; wherefore he lived until he was an hundred and forty and two years old." Verse 25 continues the count with a reign, "he reigned forty and nine years." Three numbers in two verses, and all three attach to lifespans rather than to battles.

chapter.title: A dream empties one house before the killing
chapter.text: Verse 3 moves Omer out, and verse 5 kills the son who stayed.

chapter.title: The murder happens during official business
chapter.text: Verse 5 places it on the throne, in the middle of an audience.

chapter.title: The oath turns on the man who supplied it
chapter.text: Verse 5 has Akish send the sworn men against the father-in-law who crowned him.

chapter.title: A son is starved in his father's prison
chapter.text: Verse 7 gives the whole thing in half a sentence.

chapter.title: Gain and power split the same movement
chapter.text: Verse 11 has the sons of Akish buy the people their father had bound by oath.

chapter.title: A civil war ends with a number
chapter.text: Verse 12 puts the survivors at thirty souls, plus the household that had already left.

chapter.title: Two names are left in the original
chapter.text: Verse 19 gives cureloms and cumoms without translating them, in a list where everything else is plain English.

chapter.title: Repentance is accepted at the last hour
chapter.text: Verse 34 has them turn while eating carcasses, and verse 35 sends the rain.

applications.title: Mercy sorted within one household
applications.text: The Lord was merciful to Omer and to his sons and daughters who did not seek his destruction. The qualifying clause divides a single family, which is where most of the real sorting has to happen.

applications.title: Move when you are told to move
applications.text: Omer left on a dream, and his was the household that lasted.

applications.title: Watch what an oath gets used for
applications.text: The men sworn to Akish were turned on the man who had crowned him.

applications.title: Notice when the goal changes hands
applications.text: Akish wanted power and his people wanted money. The kingdom split along that seam.

applications.title: Count what the fight costs the thing you are fighting over
applications.text: The war between Akish and his sons ran for years and destroyed nearly all the people of the kingdom, leaving thirty souls. A contest over who rules can consume the thing being ruled, and that arithmetic is almost never done beforehand.

applications.title: Some lives end in peace inside a violent book
applications.text: Emer saw peace for four years after handing over the kingdom, saw the Son of Righteousness, rejoiced, and died in peace. The surrounding chapter is a chain of murders and it still stops to record this.

applications.title: Turning late still counts
applications.text: They repented while eating carcasses, and the rain came.

applications.title: "Sufficiently" is carrying weight in that sentence
applications.text: The rain came when they had humbled themselves sufficiently before the Lord. The word admits a real threshold and declines to specify it, which is honest about how this actually goes.

questions.text: What warning have I been given that I have not acted on?
What have I agreed to that could be turned against someone I owe?
Where have I been hardest on the person closest to me?
Am I in something for a different reason than the people beside me?
What have I seen that let me rejoice in a day still coming?
Whose warning have I thrown into a pit?
How bad would it have to get before I turned?
